mcqs.question: At an ordinary point x0 of y'' + p(x)y' + q(x)y = 0, how many linearly independent power series solutions exist?
mcqs.explanation: The existence theorem guarantees exactly two linearly independent series solutions at an ordinary point, matching the order of the ODE.

whyOthersWrong.A: A second-order linear ODE has a 2-dimensional solution space.
whyOthersWrong.C: Ordinary points always admit series solutions by the existence theorem.
whyOthersWrong.D: The solution space is exactly 2-dimensional, not infinite.

mcqs.question: What does the Laplace transform turn a linear ODE with initial conditions into?

options.D: An integral equation with no closed form

mcqs.explanation: The Laplace transform converts derivatives into polynomial multiples of the transformed variable, turning the ODE into an algebraic equation in s.

whyOthersWrong.A: The transformed equation is linear and algebraic, not nonlinear.
whyOthersWrong.C: No extra spatial variable is introduced.
whyOthersWrong.D: The whole point of the method is to avoid this — it produces a closed-form algebraic equation.

mcqs.question: For (1+x^2)y''+xy'-y=0 about x0=0, what determines the radius of convergence of the power series solution?

options.A: The nearest real singular point only
options.B: The nearest singular point in the complex plane
options.C: The coefficients of the recurrence relation
options.D: Always infinity, since p,q look smooth on the real line

mcqs.explanation: The radius of convergence is governed by the nearest singularity of the coefficient functions in the COMPLEX plane (here x=±i, giving radius 1), even if none appear on the real line.

whyOthersWrong.A: Real-line-only singularities can miss closer complex singularities.
whyOthersWrong.C: The recurrence's arithmetic doesn't directly reveal the radius — the coefficient functions' singularities do.
whyOthersWrong.D: A common but incorrect assumption — see the Power Series Solutions topic page's Difficult example.
